title: Sense Perceptions
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer's main teaching emphasizes the importance of approaching zazen with an open mind, letting go of desire and ambition, and simply being present in each moment. They encourage us to cultivate a deeper awareness of our senses and experience life fully, without distraction or expectation. By doing so, we can discover that true understanding is not something we grasp intellectually, but rather it arises from our direct experience of the world, unfiltered by our own consciousness.

sentences.text: We begin again.
And I believe and I hope that we will never come to the end of beginning again.
It's great to be here.
It's good to see all of you.
You cheer up my eyes.
And it's good to enter the world of zazen.
Zazen meaning to gather the mind together.
So it's good to be here for zazen, to be quiet together, to slow the world down so we can feel what it's really like to be alive.
To me, zazen is the perfect life.
Desire is reduced.
Ambition is reduced.
And the only thing we have to worry about is this next moment to take care of with tenderness and simplicity.
So the best way to do this is just to abandon everything and try to take care of every moment that comes.
And don't worry, because there really and truly isn't anything to worry about.
Just disappear into every moment as it comes, as it goes.
Take care of your posture, take care of your breathing, take care of your thoughts, your feelings, your sensations that will come and go.
And try your best not to get caught by anything.
And should it happen that you do get caught, probably we all will, then just know.
Oh, and knowing that, you will be uncaught temporarily until the next time.
So this is a really easy practice.
Somehow it has a reputation for being very hard and severe.
But actually, nothing could be easier than this practice.
And I hope that you will all enjoy it.
You notice that the schedule is a little bit different from what we've done before.
Now we have talks in the evening as well as the morning talk.
And several of the priests who have been shuso are giving those talks and also are offering practice discussion during the day.
We're doing this because the Every Day Zen family of sanghas is changing.
Things never stay the same.
And so things are changing and our groups are maturing.
Now we have quite a few senior practitioners, people who have been doing this for a long time and have a good understanding.
And we're beginning to develop teachers.
So naturally as this process goes on, it's going to get a little confusing and difficult.
Because naturally we're going to start to map our desire and our ambition onto the whole proposition of priests and teachers and so forth.
And that will be, and it has already been, somewhat painful.
And if there was a way to avoid this, we would certainly do it.
But there isn't.
So just to note, we know this, but I'll note again that the Dharma is not the same as the world.
In the world, we award status and position to people who are talented and smart and aggressive enough to get ahead.
But in Dharma, we appreciate faith and sincerity and a visible steadiness in practice over the long haul.
The people who become priests and teachers are not, unfortunately, the most talented or the smartest.
Nor are they necessarily the best meditators or even the ones with the best Zen understanding.
And they're not even always the nicest, the most sensitive, or the kindest people that we could find.
Let's be truthful and let's not have unrealistic expectations.
However, we can expect them to be faithful to the practice and have faith in the practice.
We can expect them to be sincere in their practice and we can expect them to be steady.
We can expect them to show up time and time and time again.
And especially, we can expect them to have, as their number one priority and as their vow, that they would practice for others and with others, that we can expect.
And we should scream at them if they don't evidence these things.
In the world, we think, oh, so-and-so got promoted.
So-and-so won the prize.
But in the Dharma, we know that there is no so-and-so.
There is no separate, heroic person.
There's only our mutual co-arising.
So it would be a mistake to think that teachers are other people.
They're not.
They're us.
Teachers and students co-create each other.
There is no way that there could be one without the other.
If this week you give me your ears and your heart, I will be able to speak.
If you don't, I will move my lips, but it might not mean much.
Whatever Dharma power I can convey to you comes from you, through me to you, which is what Buddha means.
So in all this I'm just trying to say, please support the teachers that you have created and are creating.
Don't make the mistake of seeing them as others.
See them as yourself, as the fruit of your practice.
Listen to their Dharma words with a generous spirit.
And go visit them in practice discussion, because it will be good for them.
It will help them.
And if it helps you, too, that would be also excellent.
But for sure, it will be good for them.

I don't know if Every Day Zen will continue when the time comes, not so long from now, when I am no longer able to join you for practice because I'm either too decrepit to get out of bed or already dead.
So I don't know if at that time this will go on.
And I know that in the big picture of things I'm not so worried about it, because it doesn't matter much.
But the Dharma will go on, whether or not we go on.
And certainly it's obvious that there will be a time when we will not go on, whenever that time comes.
But I do think that the Every Day Zen Dharma, the Dharma of Soto Zen, of Dogen, of Suzuki Roshi, is a unique and important offering to the world.
So if possible, we should do everything that we can do so that it can continue when I can no longer continue.
And I hope that at this point we're all clear that the Every Day Zen Dharma is not the creation of one person.
It doesn't depend on one person.
There are many, many of us now who hold and convey this way of practice.
And the more we're clear about this, the more likely it is that our way will continue.
So at the outset of this sesshin, I want to encourage all of us to be very intimate in practicing with our six senses.
Like the rest of our lives, that sesshin always occurs at a time in a specific place.
And each of us is always living exactly there, at the nexus, at the meeting point, at the exact center of a specific time and place where those two meet.
And in sesshin, we have a chance to literally feel how this is so.
We can literally sense it.
This morning, I was so impressed.
I don't go to service that often.
So when I go to service, it's a revelation.
I'm amazed by the service.
So today I was really amazed by the lines that we chanted:
*Eye and sight, ear and sound, nose and smell, tongue and taste.
Thus in all things, the leaves spread from the root.
The whole process must return to the source.*
I was so inspired by those lines.

In the literal, physical, and of course it's more than physical, activity of the senses, if we can be quiet enough, if we can just for a moment let go of our constant worry about ourselves in the middle of the senses, the activity of the senses, we can experience everything we need for this whole lifetime.
So please, this week, do your best to pay very, very close attention to the exact physical and spiritual literalness of your sense experiences.
Appreciate the wonder of this specific place and time that is enacted at every moment exactly where you are.
You are in the center of it.
So please appreciate that.
Let yourself appreciate that this week.
When you have a chance to see something, and there are so many wondrous things to see around here, let yourself just see it.
When you have a chance to hear something, and there are so many beautiful things to hear around here, just let yourself hear it, completely hear it.
Try to allow yourself to go beyond your grasping and your naming to the root, to the source that is always present in each and every sensual experience.

And if you stay as close as possible to the breath, as close as possible to the feeling of the body, not only when you are sitting, but all the time, this will help you to really pay attention to each and every experience.
In most of the classical Zen stories of awakening, it almost never happens that awakening occurs during meditation.
Usually, awakening occurs with a sudden recognition in the midst of sensual experience.
One master was awakened when he heard the sound of a pebble striking a bamboo when he was sweeping a pathway.
Another one was awakened when he saw a flower.
One was awakened when someone blew out the light, leaving him in total darkness.
Many were awakened at the sound of a word, a voice, a shout.
There were a few spectacular cases of people being awakened when they were hit over the head with something or knocked down, and their body felt the shock.
So when you think about this, this is very interesting.
Awakening is not something that is produced by meditation, nor does it come in spectacular visions or states of high exaltation.
It comes from a shock of recognition in ordinary sense experience when you suddenly realize what's going on just in sense experience.

Now, when you consider the fact that we're having sense experience all the time, every day, all day long, we're always having sense experience, and we seem not to be particularly awakened by our sense experience.
In fact, for us it might be just the opposite.
We're overwhelmed and barraged by all the sensual data that comes in, oversaturated with sense experience.
And instead of awakening us, you might say, it's dulling our minds.
We're almost battered and inured to our sense experience.

So what's the difference between the kind of sense experience that awakened the ancients, the kind of sense experience that we can ourselves directly note here in sesshin, and the everyday sense perception that we experience that maybe gets us weary and fatigued?
So in Buddhist psychology, there are six senses.
Eye, sense of sight, sound, smell, taste, touch, mind.
Did I leave one out?
So mind is a sense too.
Just as the eye sees something, the mind has a thought or a feeling.
But the Buddhist analysis of sense experience is fairly complicated.
By themselves, the six senses can't do anything.
The eye in and of itself cannot see.
The ear by itself can't hear.
The nose by itself can't smell.
The sense organs require sense objects for them to be sense organs.
Sense objects activate a sense organ.
So with the six sense organs, there are six sense objects.
And these twelve together are called the twelve ayatanas, or the twelve sense spheres.
And the objects are named after the organs, the sight object, the sound object.
So eye and sight, ear and sound, nose and smell, and so forth.
Now, this seems pretty obvious in a way.
Why even bother to say it?
But when you think about it, it's not so obvious as it seems.

If I go outside here and look at one of these beautiful trees, stand in front of it, see it, hear the wind in its branches, and if I look around and make sure nobody's looking, I lick the trunk of the tree and I taste it, I might think to myself, I'm really experiencing this tree.
But that would not be exactly right.
The eye would see a sight object.
The ear would hear an ear object.
And so on.
In other words, the six senses would stream in entirely different sorts of experience.
And each of those six very different experiences would be conditioned by a set of six very different objects.
After all, if you think of an eye, the way an eye looks, the way an eye functions, it couldn't be more different from an ear, in the way an ear looks, in the way an ear functions.
And a nose couldn't be more different from a fingertip or a tongue.
And hearing is a totally different experience from seeing and tasting.
It's a completely different experience from touching and so forth.
So that's why we don't ever see music or hear a rainbow.
That's why if we hold an apple in our hand, it's a totally different experience from taking a bite out of that apple and eating it.
So each of the senses is utterly different, one from the other.
And of course we all know this.
But to really contemplate it and really understand what this makes of our lives is something else.
You become astonished by it.
The closer you get to these sense experiences, the more obvious and marvelous it is how different they are from each other.

And when you begin to appreciate sense experience at that level, it begins to dawn on you that the world that we think we're living in, the world that we have viewed quite unconsciously in a particular way, is not really that way.
I said that there are twelve.
In Buddhist psychology we use the term Ayatana, twelve Ayatanas.
And the definition of Ayatana is [unclear: "Ayya Devara"].
And Ayya means arising, that something arises as opposed to passing away, it arises.
And Devara means a door.
So the six senses and the six objects are called the twelve doors of arising, the twelve doors through which the world arises, comes to be, the twelve sources of the world.

Now, again, although we haven't thought this through, basically the way we look at it is that the world is laying out there fairly rigidly, fairly intractably, which is why our life is so difficult and why we are so powerless, the world being so weighty and large.
It's a big, bulky world out there, and we are very vulnerable within it.
But this teaching of the 12 Ayatanas says, no, that's not quite right.
The world is not a big, bulky object laying out there.
The world comes to be in the moment when there is a dynamic relation.
And the word for that relation is called sparsha, contact.

In the moment of contact between sense organ and sense object, a door opens and the world suddenly arises, the world suddenly at that moment comes to be, which is why the world is not a big, bulky something.
The world is six kinds of experiences that we are having.
These are the 12 doors that, working together, open up a world all of a sudden new.
So the world is literally you and I and our sense organs and our relationship to objects that are just as conditioned by our sense organs as our sense organs are conditioned by them.
So the world is not over there, out there, and we are not outside of the world, over here.
We are creating the world new every moment, and the world is creating us new every moment.
And there's no other world apart from this co-creation, this co-expression.
There's only an ongoing flow of six very different kinds of intimate relationships that we are misnaming and misrepresenting as a world.
But the Buddhist analysis of sense perception doesn't end there, because even the 12 ayatanas by themselves are insufficient to produce the world.
If it only went that far, six sense organs contact six sense objects, we still don't yet have a world, because there's one item missing: consciousness.

So the analysis goes on that there are 18 dhatus, 18 realms or places, and this is the 12 ayatanas plus the six consciousnesses, which of course are eye consciousness, ear consciousness, and so forth, each one completely different from the other.
A particular kind of organ makes contact with a particular matching sort of object, and a particular matching sort of consciousness arises from that.
And this experience combines with whatever other sorts of consciousness have been activated, like mind consciousness, which includes within it memory, knowledge, past experiences, and so forth.
We've put all this complex together, and we say it's the world.
So the world is actually a very rich and complex set of inward experiences, an inward set of relationships.

And the beauty of sesshin is that we can begin to experience it that way when things slow down, when the mind slows down, when we allow the experience of the senses to be just as real for us and just as primary for us as our worry about ourselves, which is usually the main thing going on.
So we hardly notice.
We notice the world is out there, but we completely subsume it under our self-worry.
This way maybe the world can tap us on the shoulder and say, "I'm glad that you stopped worrying about yourself for a moment.
Let's get together."
The Buddhist sense of what consciousness itself is, is very difficult to discern.
The word for consciousness is vijnana, which seems to mean awareness or knowing, a sense of knowing.
But the prefix vij means to cut, so it's a kind of knowing that is cut or alienated.
According to Buddhism, consciousness is the most important and the most basic thing that there is, only it's exactly not a thing.
You can't separate consciousness out from something else or define it.
Consciousness is what the world is and what we are together.
Before anything, there's already consciousness.
And that's why consciousness is said to be cut, because once there are things that seem to be apart from consciousness, then there's a knower and a known, something to be aware of.
So there's a kind of gap, a kind of cut, exile.
So someone might hear all this and say, well, that's interesting, but isn't it a little bit beside the point?
I mean, that's just the human experience of the world, but it doesn't really tell us anything about how the world really is.
So maybe we are experiencing the world, something like that, but what about the actual world itself, independent of us?
Let's think about that for a minute.
What would it be, a world completely independent of us?
Could we imagine such a thing?
Wouldn't the world without us, the objective world, automatically always be a projection of our own consciousness?
If we're the ones imagining it, how could it be otherwise?
How could we ever get outside consciousness to see a world beyond consciousness?
Maybe mathematically we could do that.
But then mathematics is more real than sense perception?
I don't know.
And then again, could there be such a thing as mathematics if there wasn't human consciousness?
Would there be a word, mathematics, without human consciousness?
So I'm not trying to say that there's no world out there apart from our relationship to it.
I don't know what's out there or not.
But I think that is the point, that we don't know.
What we do know is we are alive, and we cause a great deal of harm, and we suffer a great deal of misery.
This much we can be certain of.
And we seem to keep on doing this in the world, and we don't really know why.
Nobody likes it.
If we knew why, we would have stopped doing it long ago.

So maybe we've been paying way too much attention to outward objects, actual existence and basic nature we are quite unsure of, and way too little attention to the inward experiences we are having that in fact constitute the world that we're living in.
Obviously we have a tremendously developed material culture, and in many ways that's a blessing.
But we have a tremendously underdeveloped spiritual culture.
So this is an astonishing reality.

Is it possible that we human beings, through these many, many generations, have been obsessed with a sort of self-destructive, wrong-headed point of view that has caused us to be pursuing exactly the opposite of what we should be pursuing?
Is that possible?
Is it possible that we've been putting all this effort into running a million miles an hour in exactly the opposite direction from the one that we need to be going in?
It seems impossible that that could be so.

But when you consider the state of the world we live in, and the way that we've lived on the planet for all this time, when you consider the conduct of virtually all the governments of all the states of the world, which after all are our representatives.
They represent the thinking and the attitude and the way that we view the world.
They're analogues of that for us.
They're projections of our inner way of looking at things.
When you consider all this, you can almost believe that that might be true, that we've been going in the wrong direction very quickly.
The Buddha didn't consider himself to be a philosopher.
Certainly he was not a scientist.
He was not, in other words, concerned to ascertain the nature of things or to understand how this world works.
He mostly saw himself as a doctor, as a healer, and his goal was the alleviation of human suffering.

The Buddhist analysis of perception was established for the purpose of reorienting us in our living, so that we could once and for all let go of our obsessive outward focus, not because it's immoral, unspiritual, not because it's incorrect even, but because it's destructive to us.
We create a world apart from us at our own peril.
We create a world apart from us at the world's peril.
So let's now go back to the Zen Masters and their awakening.

If the world and we are creating each other all the time, and if the intimate experiences of seeing and hearing and smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking, feeling, equal, thinking, feeling, seeing, hearing, touching, tasting equal, if these experiences are all intimate and unique and could only occur with the world, then knowing this ourselves firsthand would really be a revelation, because we would no longer feel alone and vulnerable.
We would not be so weary of our humanness all the time, the feeling that we are not enough, that we need to have or to be or to know or to experience something more.
We would not have that feeling.
We would instead say, as the Buddha said when he was awakened by the sense experience of seeing a star in the sky, "How marvelous, how marvelous," he said.
"All things in this moment are completely awake.
All things are awake," he said.
Not, "I am awake."
Too bad about all these other people.
But how wonderful.
All things are awake in this moment, and they are beautiful and complete.
When we see the world, we don't see that.
We look at the world and we see our own need, our own desire, our own frustration, our own fear.
And this is the supreme irony.
However much we have thought this through, we are all convinced that there is a big bad world out there and there is poor us over here.
And because of this viewpoint, when we look at the world, we don't see a world.
We see the wounded insides of our own heart.
That's what we see when we look out at the world.
Unlike us, the Zen masters of old knew that there is no world out there.
And there is no heroic individual over here.
And so they could see the world as it really is, as awake, as intimate, as essentially joyful.
Now if you study the sayings and doings of the old masters, you realize after a while, when you get over the strangeness of the Chinese literary style, how different they all were from one another.
Some of them were happy-go-lucky trickster types.
Some of them were very serious pious types, even to the point of being grim and ungenerous.
Some were deep and profound, and some were always fooling around.
So they were all quite different in their personalities.
But all of them shared a tremendous love for the world.
And each of them, because of that love, discovered the way for each one, for him or her, to be in the world, the right way for this one or that one to be in the world.
And they all cared deeply about the world and about others.
And that's why, like the Buddha, they dedicated themselves to trying to encourage others to practice.
And most of them, maybe all of them, spent their entire lives just like the Buddha, practicing with others many, many years.

So I'm not trying to say that we all should be Zen Masters, or we all even have to be Buddhists, only that if any one of us is going to have any hope of really being happy, really being sane, in this crazy world, in this lifetime, and if the world is going to survive in any reasonable way outside of all the dystopian nightmare movies and books we all are now taking in, then all of us and each of us is going to have to change the way we view the world and the way we live in it.
We're going to have to realize that the world is our best friend, that the world is closer to us, literally closer to us than we are to ourselves.
And we're going to have to see that there's nothing to fear, that there are no enemies, and this is the hardest of all, to understand that absolutely nothing can harm us.
When we see this, we can be happy.
And when enough of us see this, the whole world is going to be really different.
So I'll close my talk today with a poem of Dogen.
He says:

*I strain my ears, raise my head, and wait for the dawn breeze, how many times dreamily herding an ox in the spring rain, who realizes that this intention pierces the heavens, just remain with rising eyebrows and blinking eyes.

I strain my ears, raise my head, and wait for the dawn breeze, how many times dreamily herding an ox in the spring rain, who realizes that this intention pierces the heavens, just remain with rising eyebrows and blinking eyes.*
